subsection: 4. Environmentally responsible practices in the home

notes.b: Everyday household activities use energy, water and materials, and generate emissions and waste. The impact of each activity depends on how much energy it uses and which fuel supplies that energy.
points: Space heating and hot water account for the largest share of energy use in most homes.
Electricity used in the home is generated partly by burning fossil fuels, releasing carbon dioxide at the power station.
Water used in the home must be pumped and treated, and hot water also needs energy to heat it.
Packaging, food waste and discarded appliances all add to the waste that is landfilled or recovered.
Heat escapes through the roof, walls, floor and windows; insulation laid on the floor of the roof space is one of the most effective measures for an existing house.
Cavity wall insulation fills the gap between the two leaves of a masonry wall, reducing heat loss through the walls.
Draught-proofing seals gaps around doors, windows, letterboxes and floorboards, which stops warm air escaping and cold air entering.
Double or triple glazing reduces heat loss through windows; closing thick curtains at night adds a further layer of insulation.
A lagging jacket on the hot water cylinder and insulated pipes reduce heat lost while water is stored and moved.
A room thermostat and a programmer ensure that the heating runs only when it is needed; lowering the set temperature, even slightly, reduces fuel use.
Thermostatic radiator valves control the temperature of individual radiators, so unused rooms can be kept cooler.
Reflective panels behind radiators on external walls send heat back into the room rather than into the wall.
An annual boiler service keeps combustion efficient so that less fuel is burned for the same heat.
Renewable heat sources, such as heat pumps, solar thermal panels and stoves burning wood from sustainably managed forests, reduce reliance on fossil fuels.
Heating the water accounts for most of the energy used by a washing machine on a hot wash.
A cold or 30 °C wash uses far less energy than a 60 °C or 90 °C wash, and modern detergents clean well at lower temperatures.
A full load uses almost the same energy and water as a part load, so run the machine only when it is full.
An eco programme runs at lower temperatures or with less water, using less energy per load.
A higher spin speed removes more water before drying, which reduces the time a dryer must run.
A tumble dryer is one of the most energy-intensive appliances in the home, so line drying saves significant energy.
Using the correct dose of detergent avoids residue in the water and reduces the amount of product that enters drains.
Food waste sent to landfill decomposes anaerobically and releases methane, a greenhouse gas.
Food production uses land, water, fertiliser and energy, so wasted food wastes all the resources used to grow, transport and package it.
Plan meals and buy only what will be eaten; use leftovers and freeze surplus food promptly.
Store food correctly: keep the fridge at or below 5 °C, and freeze food at -18 °C or below, which slows bacterial growth and preserves it.
Vegetables, pulses and cereals generally need less land, water and energy to produce than meat and dairy, so eating more plant-based foods lowers the environmental impact of the diet.
Seasonal and local food avoids the energy used for long-distance transport and for heated or refrigerated storage and growing.
Buy loose fruit and vegetables and products with minimal packaging, and use a reusable bag and containers for bulk and counter purchases.
The EU energy label rates an appliance from A to G for energy efficiency; A-rated appliances are the most efficient.
The label also shows the appliance's annual energy consumption and its noise level.
For washing machines and dishwashers, the label shows water use as well.
Choosing a model with a higher rating and the right capacity for the household gives the lowest energy use; an oversized appliance uses more energy than its load needs.
Standby mode draws electricity continuously; switch appliances off at the socket, or use a switched power strip.
LED bulbs use much less power than incandescent bulbs and last much longer.
Use the oven only when needed, avoid preheating for longer than necessary, and use a microwave or slow cooker for small quantities.
Boil only the water needed in a kettle.
Clogged filters and dirty condenser coils make fridges and dryers use more energy; keep them clean.
A fridge set colder than necessary wastes energy, and a freezer that is not kept full uses more energy to stay cold.
Keeping a working appliance in use through servicing, repair or second-hand sale avoids the energy and materials needed to manufacture a replacement.
Shorter showers use less hot water than baths, and so less energy is needed for heating.
Turning off the tap while brushing teeth and fixing dripping taps save water that would otherwise be wasted.
A dual-flush toilet allows the smaller flush to be used for liquid waste, saving water with each flush.
Collecting rainwater in a butt provides free water for the garden.

keyTerms.definition: The escape of heat from a building through its roof, walls, floor, windows and gaps.
Sealing gaps around doors, windows and floors to stop warm air escaping and cold air entering.
Insulating material placed in the gap between the two leaves of a masonry wall to reduce heat loss.
Insulating material wrapped around a hot water cylinder or pipes to reduce heat loss.
A valve that controls the heat output of an individual radiator according to the room temperature.
The EU label rating an appliance's energy efficiency from A to G, with its annual energy consumption and noise level.
The electricity an appliance keeps drawing while it appears switched off but remains plugged in and in standby mode.
A washing machine setting that uses less energy or water, usually by running at a lower temperature for longer.
Food that is discarded rather than eaten, which wastes the resources used to produce it and releases methane when landfilled.
Food that is grown and harvested at its natural time of year, which avoids energy used in heated or refrigerated growing and storage.

factCards.term: Four measures to cut heat loss from the home
factCards.definition: Roof and attic insulation; cavity wall insulation; double or triple glazing; draught-proofing.

factCards.term: Three ways a thermostat and programmer save energy
factCards.definition: They stop the heating running when the house is empty; they keep rooms at the set temperature rather than overheating them; they allow unused rooms to be kept cooler.

factCards.term: Four washing machine settings that save energy
factCards.definition: A lower wash temperature; full loads only; an eco programme; a higher spin speed.

factCards.term: Three reasons food waste harms the environment
factCards.definition: It releases methane when landfilled; it wastes the energy and water used to produce it; it wastes the energy used to transport and package it.

factCards.term: Three benefits of seasonal and local food
factCards.definition: Less energy for long-distance transport; less packaging needed for shipping; less energy for heated or refrigerated growing and storage.

factCards.term: Four pieces of information on an EU energy label
factCards.definition: Energy efficiency rating from A to G; annual energy consumption; noise level; water use for washing machines and dishwashers.

factCards.term: Two steps to reduce the energy used by a fridge
factCards.definition: Keep it at or below 5 °C rather than colder; keep its filters and condenser coils clean.

factCards.term: Two reasons to repair an appliance rather than replace it
factCards.definition: It keeps the appliance in use for longer; it avoids the energy and materials needed to manufacture a new one.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways a household can reduce the energy used for heating, and explain the environmental benefit of each.
questions.model: Two correctly described measures, each with its benefit. Examples: insulating the roof or walls, which reduces the heat lost and so the fuel burned, lowering carbon dioxide emissions; draught-proofing, which stops warm air escaping and reduces fuel use; fitting a programmer and thermostats, so that the heating runs only when needed; servicing the boiler, so that fuel burns more completely. Each measure must be linked to a reduction in fuel use or emissions.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the choices a household makes about heating, washing clothes, food and appliances affect the environment. Recommend a practical change in each area and explain its environmental benefit.
questions.model: Heating: heat escapes through the roof, walls, floor and windows; burning fuel for heat releases carbon dioxide; recommend insulation or draught-proofing with the benefit of less fuel burned, plus a programmer and thermostat. Washing clothes: heating water uses most of the energy in a hot wash; recommend a cold or 30 degree wash, or an eco programme, with the benefit of less energy used and less detergent entering waterways; line drying avoids the energy used by a dryer. Food: food waste releases methane in landfill and wastes the resources used to produce it; recommend planning meals and buying only what will be eaten, with the benefit of fewer resources wasted; eating more plant-based foods reduces land, water and energy use. Appliances: choose a highly rated appliance on the EU energy label with the right capacity; switch off standby power; keeping working appliances in use avoids the energy used to make replacements. Each recommendation must be linked to its environmental benefit.
